items.t: Inside the Operating Theatre — Maintaining the Sterile Field
items.c: How to keep the sterile field sterile throughout an operation.
Monopolar: current leaves the active electrode, passes through the patient and returns by the return pad.
A quick list on return pad: where and how: Large, well-perfused muscular area close to the surgical site; Clean, dry, hairless skin.
Cut: continuous waveform that cuts cleanly with little coagulation.
A quick list on why diathermy burns happen: Poor return-pad contact or a wet pad site; Pooled prep fluid under the patient.
Alcohol-based skin prep is flammable.
A quick list on the theatre fire triangle: OXYGEN: enriched oxygen and nitrous oxide help fire spread; IGNITION: diathermy, laser, fibre-optic light cable.
Smoke from diathermy and lasers contains particles, chemicals and sometimes biological material.
Diathermy can interfere with a pacemaker or ICD.
Ultrasonic scalpels use blade vibration (around 55 kHz) to cut and seal, with less lateral heat spread than monopolar.
Argon gas flows over a monopolar current and carries it to the tissue without touching it.
Two widely used steam cycles are about 121 °C (roughly 15 to 30 minutes) and about 134 °C (roughly 3 to 4 minutes for unwrapped, longer for wrapped loads).
Run in an empty pre-vacuum steam steriliser before the first load of the day.
Chemical indicators change colour when exposed to certain conditions.
A quick list on wet packs are not sterile: Moisture lets microbes travel through wrapping; Causes: overloaded trays, wrong packing, poor drying.
Unwrapped steam sterilisation for an instrument needed at once.
A quick list on sterilisation does not clean: Blood and tissue protect microbes from steam; Pre-clean at the point of use. Do not let blood dry.
The cleaner uses high-frequency sound to create tiny bubbles that lift debris from crevices.
Items that cannot take steam may use ethylene oxide or hydrogen peroxide gas plasma.

items.t: How long does a sterile pack stay sterile?
items.c: Many guidelines treat sterility as event-related: the pack stays sterile until its integrity is compromised (torn, wet, dropped, opened).
Prions resist ordinary sterilisation.
Capnography shows each breath.
A quick list on limits of pulse oximetry: SpO2 is normally 95 to 100 percent; It lags behind real changes in oxygenation.
Common volatile agents include sevoflurane, isoflurane and desflurane.
A quick list on when the oxygen supply fails: Switch to the backup cylinder on the machine; Check the cylinder has enough contents before every list.

items.t: Medical gas colours differ by country
items.c: Colour codes for gas cylinders follow national or regional standards.
Anaesthesia widens blood vessels and moves heat from the core to the skin.
A quick list on malignant hyperthermia: first signs: Rising end-tidal CO2 despite good ventilation; Fast heart rate and stiff jaw muscles (masseter spasm).
A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high reading.
A cannula in an artery connects to a pressure transducer.
Laryngospasm: the vocal cords close.

items.t: Arm abduction and the brachial plexus
items.c: Arms on boards abducted beyond 90 degrees or pulled back can stretch the brachial plexus.
The ulnar nerve runs close to the skin behind the elbow.

items.t: Common peroneal nerve and foot drop
items.c: The common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular head below the knee.
A quick list on lithotomy position risks: Nerve injury in the legs from stirrup pressure; Compartment syndrome in long cases.
Head-down tilt raises venous return but also pressure in the head and eyes.
In sitting or beach-chair positions the surgical site can be above the heart.
A quick list on prone position checks: Eyes free of any pressure (corneal injury and vision loss risk); Neck in a neutral line.
Pressure injuries form over bony areas such as the sacrum, heels and back of the head.

items.t: Lateral position and the axillary roll
items.c: A roll is placed just below the armpit, supporting the chest wall so that the weight of the chest does not press on the lower arm and nerves.
A quick list on moving the unconscious patient: The anaesthetist controls the head and airway; At least four people for an adult in most settings.
Swabs are the most commonly retained items.
A quick list on count rules that work: Count aloud, together, in the same order every time; No swabs or sharps leave the room.
The checklist has 19 items in three phases: Sign In (before anaesthesia), Time Out (before incision) and Sign Out (before the patient leaves the room).
A quick list on what the time out confirms: Team members introduce themselves by name and role; Patient, procedure and site are confirmed aloud.
A quick list on sharps safety: Pass sharps in a neutral zone or tray, not hand to hand; Never recap a needle.
Latex allergy can range from skin reactions to life-threatening anaphylaxis.
Reduce time in the beam, stand as far away as possible and use shielding.
A quick list on laser safety: Everyone in the room wears eyewear rated for that laser's wavelength; Warning signs on the door.
Label specimens in theatre, aloud with the surgeon, before they leave the room.

items.t: Chlorhexidine or iodine for skin prep
items.c: Both chlorhexidine-alcohol and povidone-iodine reduce skin bacteria, and many guidelines favour chlorhexidine-alcohol for most surgery.
Adult laparoscopy usually keeps intra-abdominal pressure around 12 to 15 mmHg.
Carbon dioxide does not support combustion and is absorbed and cleared quickly if it enters a vessel.
Closed entry uses a Veress needle with safety checks before insufflation.
A quick list on camera and scope care: White-balance with white gauze before insertion; Warm the lens or use anti-fog to prevent fogging.
The tip of a fibre-optic cable carries intense light that can burn skin and ignite drapes within seconds.
A quick list on laparoscopic complications to know: Bowel or vascular injury at entry; Gas embolism (rare).
Flexible endoscopes are cleaned by hand, leak-tested and then high-level disinfected or sterilised depending on use.
Saline is used with bipolar equipment.
During transurethral resection, large volumes of non-electrolyte fluid can be absorbed.
Common laparoscopic ports are 5 mm, 10 to 11 mm and 12 mm.
Polyglactin 910 (Vicryl) is absorbed in roughly two to three months.

items.t: Suture sizes: more zeros, thinner thread
items.c: Sizes such as 3-0 and 6-0 get thinner as the number before the zero rises.
A quick list on needle types: Round-bodied (tapered): soft tissues such as bowel; Conventional cutting: tough tissues such as skin.
Grasp the needle roughly one-third to one-half of the way from the swage (thread end) towards the tip, at right angles to the jaws.
A flat square knot is the base.
Gelatin sponge, oxidised cellulose, bone wax and fibrin sealants help control oozing.
Sutures, staples, tissue adhesive and adhesive strips each suit different wounds.
A quick list on four phases of wound healing: Haemostasis: bleeding stops, clot forms; Inflammation: cells clear debris, often first days.
A passive drain such as a Penrose lets fluid flow out by gravity and capillary action.
A dressing protects the wound from contamination, absorbs fluid and supports it.
Many protocols set tourniquet pressure from the limb occlusion pressure (the pressure that stops arterial flow) plus a safety margin, rather than a single fixed number.
Raising the limb and wrapping with an Esmarch bandage drains blood before inflation to give a dry field.

items.t: What happens when the tourniquet comes down
items.c: After release, blood flows back into the limb.
A quick list on urinary catheter points: Typical adult sizes are 14 to 16 Fr. Larger and three-way types are used for irrigation; Aseptic technique and lubricant.
Bubbling in the water seal chamber suggests an air leak.
A quick list on blood transfusion safety checks: Two trained people check patient, blood group and unit number; Start a unit soon after it leaves controlled storage.
Heavy bleeding can lead to hypothermia, acidosis and clotting failure, each making the others worse.
Blood from the surgical field is collected, washed and returned to the patient.
During cementing, some patients develop low blood pressure, low oxygen or even cardiac arrest.
A frozen section lets a pathologist examine tissue while the patient is under anaesthesia, often in about 20 to 30 minutes.
Surgical hand preparation can be done with a surgical scrub or an alcohol-based hand rub, depending on product guidance.
Closed gloving keeps hands inside the gown sleeves while donning gloves.
Prophylactic antibiotics are generally given within 60 minutes before incision so that levels in tissue are high at the start.
A quick list on wound classes: Clean: no entry into hollow organs, no inflammation; Clean-contaminated: entry into a controlled organ such as bowel or airway.
Many theatres use positive-pressure ventilation so air flows outward when the door opens.
If hair removal is needed, use clippers just before the operation.
A quick list on rules of the sterile field: Sterile items stay above table height; A sterile field is never left unattended or uncovered.
Clean high-touch surfaces and anything visibly soiled with approved disinfectant between patients.
Take off the most contaminated items first.
Theatre waste is separated into general, infectious, sharps and sometimes pharmaceutical or anatomical streams.
Common triggers include neuromuscular blockers, antibiotics, latex and chlorhexidine.
Early symptoms can include a metallic taste, ringing in the ears, numbness around the mouth and confusion, followed by seizures and heart rhythm problems.
Signs: a sudden fall in ETCO2, drop in blood pressure and sometimes a churning heart murmur.
A quick list on the difficult airway trolley: Know where the trolley is before the case; Laryngoscope blades, bougie, supraglottic airways.

items.t: Cardiac arrest in theatre: think reversible causes
items.c: A quick list on cardiac arrest in theatre: think reversible causes: Hypoxia and hypovolaemia; Electrolyte problems, hypothermia.
Signs: sudden low blood pressure, high airway pressure and reduced breath sounds on one side, sometimes with a deviated trachea.
A quick list on haemorrhage classes: Class I: up to 15 percent blood loss, usually few signs; Class II: 15 to 30 percent, fast heart rate.
Common fasting guidance for elective surgery is about six hours for solids and two hours for clear fluids.
Suxamethonium can cause a sharp rise in blood potassium in some patients.
Four risk factors: female sex, non-smoker, history of PONV or motion sickness and expected post-operative opioids.
McBurney's point lies about one-third of the way along the line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.
The classic triangle is formed by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the edge of the liver.
A quick list on layers of the abdominal wall: Skin, then fatty and membranous layers of subcutaneous tissue; Three muscle layers: external oblique, internal oblique, t...
The inferior epigastric vessels are the key landmark.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the groove between the trachea and oesophagus, close to the inferior thyroid artery.
Borders: inguinal ligament above, sartorius on the outside and adductor longus on the inside.
The surgeon clamps the hepatoduodenal ligament, which carries the hepatic artery, portal vein and bile duct, to reduce blood flow to the liver.
The superior mesenteric artery supplies the small bowel and the colon up to about the splenic flexure.
In the pelvis, the ureter passes under the uterine artery.
A line between the top of the iliac crests (Tuffier's line) crosses roughly the L4 spine or L4-L5 space in adults.
Propofol is a common intravenous induction drug.
Ketamine gives pain relief and anaesthesia while usually keeping airway reflexes and blood pressure better than many other drugs.
Suxamethonium is a depolarising relaxant with a very short action.
A quick list on suxamethonium: key points: Onset in about 30 to 60 seconds and short duration; May cause muscle pains and fasciculations.
Fentanyl and morphine are common opioids.
Typical maximum doses are about 3 mg/kg for plain lignocaine, about 7 mg/kg with adrenaline, and about 2 mg/kg for bupivacaine.
Adrenaline narrows blood vessels, which prolongs the block, reduces bleeding and slows absorption of the drug.
Many people labelled as penicillin allergic are not truly allergic.
Tranexamic acid reduces breakdown of clots and lowers blood loss in surgery, trauma and postpartum bleeding.
Oxytocin makes the uterus contract after delivery.
Spinal: a small dose goes into the cerebrospinal fluid below the cord.
A quick list on common effects of a spinal: Fall in blood pressure and slow heart rate; Nausea, often from low blood pressure.
The headache is usually worse sitting or standing and better lying flat.

items.t: When not to do an epidural
items.c: A quick list on when not to do an epidural: The patient refuses; Infection at the puncture site or severe infection in the blood.
Ultrasound guidance helps show the nerve and the spread of the drug.
A quick list on brachial plexus block approaches: Interscalene: shoulder surgery. Often paralyses the diaphragm on that side; Supraclavicular: whole arm.
A caudal block puts local anaesthetic into the epidural space through the opening at the bottom of the sacrum.
A quick list on dermatome levels for surgery: T4: nipple line. Needed for caesarean section; T10: umbilicus.
Local infiltration and field blocks such as the transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block numb the abdominal wall.
The limb is emptied of blood, a tourniquet is inflated and local anaesthetic is injected into a vein.
A quick list on layers in a caesarean section: Skin and fat; Rectus sheath, then the muscles are separated, not cut.
A quick list on caesarean urgency categories: Category 1: immediate threat to the life of mother or baby; Category 2: maternal or fetal compromise, not immediately lif...
In late pregnancy the uterus can press on the vena cava and reduce blood return to the heart.
PPH is often defined as more than 500 mL after vaginal birth or 1000 mL after caesarean.
A quick list on uterotonic drugs: Oxytocin: usual first choice; Ergometrine: avoid in hypertension.
An ectopic pregnancy most often implants in the fallopian tube.
A quick list on routes for hysterectomy: Abdominal: open incision; Vaginal: no abdominal cut.
Magnesium sulphate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures.
A quick list on newborn resuscitation basics: Dry, warm and stimulate the baby; Open the airway and give ventilation if the baby is not breathing well.
A cerclage is a stitch placed around the cervix to prevent it opening too early in some pregnancies.

items.t: Children are not small adults: the airway
items.c: Children have a larger head and tongue, a narrower nose, a higher larynx and a shorter trachea.
One common formula for children aged 1 to 10 is weight in kg = (age in years + 4) × 2.
A rule of thumb for children over one year: uncuffed tube size = age ÷ 4 + 4.
Babies lose heat fast because they have a large surface area and little fat.
A quick list on paediatric fasting guidance: Solid food and formula milk: often about 6 hours; Breast milk: often about 4 hours.
Some children wake up agitated, crying and difficult to console, most often preschool age after sevoflurane.
Normal resting heart rate falls with age.

items.t: Low blood sugar in small children
items.c: Babies and young children have small glucose stores and can become hypoglycaemic with fasting, cold or illness.
Babies with pyloric stenosis have projectile vomiting.
Children's doses are calculated by weight, so a decimal point error can give ten times the dose.
An open fracture has a wound connecting to the broken bone.
A quick list on compartment syndrome: Pain out of proportion, especially on passive stretching; Tense swollen limb.
Fat droplets can enter the circulation after fractures of long bones, usually 24 to 72 hours later.
Operating on a hip fracture within about 36 to 48 hours of admission is linked to better outcomes in older patients.
Plaster is exothermic: it warms as it sets.
Power tools generate heat that can damage bone cells.
Cemented implants fix immediately and are often used in older patients with weaker bone.
A quick list on using the c-arm safely: Keep the X-ray tube below the table when possible; Stay behind a lead screen or as far away as you can.
A tourniquet may be used for limb amputations except in vascular disease.
Spinal levels are easy to miscount.
A small incision (often Lanz or gridiron) is made over the right lower abdomen.
Mesh repairs have lower recurrence than suture-only repairs for most adult hernias.
A quick list on laparoscopic cholecystectomy steps: Enter and create the pneumoperitoneum; Expose Calot's triangle and get the critical view of safety.
A quick list on common abdominal incisions: Midline: fast and flexible, little blood loss; Pfannenstiel: low transverse, used in pelvic surgery.
A quick list on bowel anastomosis principles: Good blood supply to both ends; No tension on the join.
An ileostomy (small bowel) is usually on the right and spouted, with liquid output.
The patient lies supine with a roll under the shoulders and the head supported on a ring.
A quick list on tracheostomy tube safety: Know the tube type: cuffed, uncuffed, with or without an inner tube; Keep a spare tube of the same size and one size smaller...
Axillary surgery can disturb lymph drainage and increase the risk of arm swelling.
A commonly used estimate is 4 mL × weight in kg × percentage of body surface burned, given over 24 hours.
A quick list on scalpel blade numbers: No. 10: large curved blade for skin; No. 11: pointed blade for stabs and incisions.
Mosquito forceps are small and fine.
Toothed forceps (such as Adson) grip skin and fascia firmly.
Mayo scissors are heavier and used for cutting sutures and tough tissue.
Handheld retractors (Langenbeck, Deaver, Morris) are held by an assistant.
Needle holders have short jaws that grip the needle and a ratchet that locks.
A quick list on suction tips: Yankauer: wide bore, general use and mouth; Poole: abdominal surgery, with side holes to avoid sucking up bowel.
Babcock forceps are gentle and used to hold bowel.
A quick list on bone instruments: Osteotome and chisel: cut and shape bone; Rongeur: nibbles bone away.
A quick list on caring for instruments: Do not soak in saline, because it corrodes stainless steel; Rinse blood off promptly.
A quick list on anaesthetic to recovery handover: Patient name, procedure and any problems; Airway, oxygen and breathing.
The Aldrete score rates activity, breathing, circulation, consciousness and oxygen saturation, each from 0 to 2.
Snoring means the airway is partially blocked by the tongue or soft tissue.
A 0 to 10 scale works for many adults.

items.t: Urine output as a vital sign
items.c: A usual target is at least 0.5 mL per kg per hour in adults.
A quick list on signs of bleeding after surgery: Fast heart rate, often the first sign; Restlessness, anxiety and cold, clammy skin.
Redness, heat, swelling, pain, discharge and fever.
A quick list on blood clot prevention: Early walking and leg movement; Compression stockings or calf pumps.
Consent is valid when the patient understands the procedure, the risks and the alternatives, decides freely and has the capacity to decide.
A quick list on pre-operative readiness check: ID band, consent form and the site marked; Fasting status and allergies.
Many guidelines favour a restrictive approach: transfuse stable patients when haemoglobin falls below about 7 g/dL, and around 8 g/dL for patients with heart disease.
Group and save: the lab tests the patient's blood group and keeps the sample for quick crossmatching.
A quick list on clotting tests explained: PT or INR: monitors warfarin and the extrinsic pathway; aPTT: monitors heparin and the intrinsic pathway.
High potassium can cause tall peaked T waves, a widened QRS complex and dangerous heart rhythms.
A quick list on arterial blood gas basics: pH: normal around 7.35 to 7.45; PaCO2: about 35 to 45 mmHg.

items.t: Blood glucose and diabetes in theatre
items.c: Diabetic patients need glucose checks before, during and after surgery.
Bone and metal appear white.
Ultrasound guides nerve blocks, line placement and some surgery.
Creatinine and urea rise when the kidneys do not clear waste well.
In women of child-bearing age, many hospitals check for pregnancy before surgery, especially with X-rays or certain drugs, to avoid harming an early pregnancy.
The surgeon and the anaesthetist share the airway.
Pulling on the eye muscles or pressing on the eye can trigger a reflex that slows the heart rate and may cause pauses.
Cataract surgery is often done under topical or local anaesthesia with a microscope and a phacoemulsification machine.
Head pins in a clamp hold the skull still.
Cystoscopy looks inside the bladder with a rigid or flexible scope.
Before clamping a major artery, heparin is usually given to stop clots forming.
A split-thickness graft takes part of the skin layer.
A nasal tube is often used to keep the mouth free.
On cardiopulmonary bypass the blood is drawn out of the body, oxygenated and returned.
A double-lumen tube or a bronchial blocker lets the anaesthetist ventilate one lung while the surgeon works on the other.
A quick list on suction not working: Check the canister lid is on and sealed; Look for kinks, disconnections and blocked tubing.
A quick list on diathermy gives no output: Is the return pad connected and the plug fully in?; Is the correct mode and power selected?.
A quick list on laparoscopic image problems: No picture: check the camera, cables and monitor input; Dark picture: check the light cable and light source.

High pressure alarms can mean kinks, secretions, coughing or bronchospasm.
Confirm the drug, the concentration, the rate and the patient.
Check the battery, the pads and cables, the printer paper and a self-test.
A forced-air warmer must be used with its blanket.
A quick list on ecg trace problems: Poor skin contact or dry gel: check electrodes; Movement or shivering: wait or reposition.
Scialytic lights are positioned and focused before the patient is draped.

items.t: The five moments for hand hygiene
items.c: A quick list on the five moments for hand hygiene: Before touching a patient; Before a clean or aseptic procedure.

C.
Active pulmonary TB spreads by tiny airborne droplets.
Approximate risk after a needle-stick from an infected patient: hepatitis B around 6 to 30 percent if unvaccinated, hepatitis C about 2 percent, HIV about 0.3 percent.

A quick list on theatre attire rules: Clean scrubs worn only in the theatre suite; Cap covers all hair and the mask covers nose and mouth.
Overuse of antibiotics breeds resistant bacteria.
The standard hepatitis B vaccine course is three doses, commonly at 0, 1 and 6 months.
A quick list on keeping good records: Write at the time or as soon as possible afterwards; Legible, signed, dated and timed.
In many safety programmes the phrase CUS gives a simple script: I am Concerned.
Patient information is shared only with those who need it for care.
Do only what you have been trained and authorised to do.
A quick list on sbar handover: Situation: who and what is happening now; Background: history and relevant details.
Check the consent form, mark the site with the surgeon's initials while the patient is awake where possible, and verify at the Time Out against the notes and images.
Reporting near misses, errors and equipment faults helps the team find the cause and fix it.

items.t: When a patient dies in theatre
items.c: Handle the body with respect, follow the legal and hospital procedures and support the family and the team.
A quick list on putting the patient at ease: Greet the patient by name and introduce yourself; Explain what you are doing before you do it.
Photos and videos of patients or theatre cases need clear written consent and hospital permission.
A quick list on the abcde approach: Airway: open and clear?; Breathing: rate, effort, oxygen level.
Adult compressions go about 100 to 120 per minute and about 5 to 6 cm deep, allowing the chest to recoil fully.
If the patient can cough, encourage coughing.
A quick list on first aid for burns: Stop the burning and remove clothing and jewellery that is not stuck; Cool with running water for about 20 minutes.
A quick list on controlling severe bleeding: Apply firm direct pressure with a clean pad; Raise the limb if possible.
A quick list on types of shock: Hypovolaemic: blood or fluid loss; Cardiogenic: pump failure.
A quick list on seizure first aid: Protect the person from injury and time the seizure; Nothing in the mouth.
Signs include sweating, shakiness, confusion and reduced consciousness.
If a spinal injury is possible, keep the head, neck and trunk in line.
Lay the person on their side with the upper leg bent so the body cannot roll, and the head tilted back slightly with the mouth facing down.
Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.
Oxygen delivery depends on cardiac output and the oxygen content of arterial blood.
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is roughly diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure, or (systolic + 2 × diastolic) ÷ 3.
Total body water is about 60 percent of body weight in an adult male.
Normal saline contains more chloride than plasma.
Breathing controls carbon dioxide (respiratory).
The curve shifts right (more oxygen released to tissues) with acidosis, a high CO2, fever and raised 2,3-DPG.
The healthy glomerular filtration rate is roughly 90 to 120 mL per minute.
Surgery triggers the release of cortisol and adrenaline.
Pain signals travel from nociceptors by A-delta fibres (fast, sharp pain) and C fibres (slow, dull pain) to the spinal cord and then to the brain.
Most patients should continue their usual blood pressure medicines.
Fasting and surgery change sugar levels.
Asthma patients should continue their inhalers, including on the day of surgery.
Low oxygen, dehydration, cold, acidosis and infection can trigger sickling and painful crises.
A quick list on types of anaemia: Iron deficiency: most common, small pale red cells; Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency: large red cells.
Active malaria can cause fever, anaemia, low platelets and organ problems.
Patients living with HIV receive the same standard precautions as everyone else.
TB most often affects the lungs but can involve the spine (Pott's disease), lymph nodes, bones and other organs.
Exercise capacity is a guide to heart risk.
Obese patients may be harder to ventilate by mask and desaturate faster.
A 1 percent solution contains 1 g in 100 mL, which is 10 mg per mL.
Adrenaline 1:1000 contains 1 mg per mL.
Volume to give = (dose wanted ÷ dose available) × volume it is in.
Drops per minute = (volume in mL × drop factor) ÷ time in minutes.
Rate in mL per hour = volume ÷ time in hours.
Multiply the dose per kg by the patient's weight.
A quick list on unit conversions: 1 g = 1000 mg; 1 mg = 1000 micrograms.
BMI = weight in kg ÷ (height in metres squared).
Concentration = amount of drug ÷ volume.
Fahrenheit = Celsius × 9 ÷ 5 + 32.
A quick list on prefixes you will meet daily: hyper- is above or too much. hypo- is below or too little; tachy- is fast. brady- is slow.
A quick list on operation word endings: -ectomy: removal (appendicectomy); -otomy: cutting open (laparotomy).
NPO means nothing by mouth.
A quick list on directional terms: Superior is toward the head and inferior toward the feet; Anterior is front and posterior is back.
A quick list on body planes: Sagittal: divides left and right; Coronal (frontal): divides front and back.
A quick list on well-known procedure names: Whipple procedure: pancreaticoduodenectomy; Hartmann's procedure: sigmoid removal with an end colostomy.
A quick list on wound complication words: Dehiscence: the wound splits open; Evisceration: bowel pushes out through the wound.
A quick list on endoscopy word family: Laparoscopy: looks inside the abdomen; Laparotomy: open abdominal operation.

A quick list on bleeding terms: Epistaxis: nose bleed; Haematuria: blood in the urine.
A quick list on theatre zones: Unrestricted: street clothes allowed; Semi-restricted: scrubs and caps, storage and corridors.
A quick list on power failure plan: Know where the emergency lights and torches are; Backup generator or battery systems should start.
Wall outlets and area valves control oxygen, air, nitrous oxide and suction.
Put new stock behind older stock so the oldest is used first.

items.t: Order of cases on a list
items.c: Lists are often planned with children, diabetic patients and latex-allergic patients first.
Turnover is the time between one patient leaving and the next arriving.
Sterile stores should be clean, dry, dust-free and temperature controlled, with items off the floor and away from sinks and pipes.
A quick list on emergency theatre readiness: A theatre kept ready with a checked anaesthetic machine; Crash trolley, defibrillator and difficult airway trolley.
Used instruments go from the theatre to decontamination, then inspection and packing, then sterilisation and storage.
A quick list on who does what in theatre: Surgeon and assistant: the operation; Anaesthetist and assistant: the patient's airway, breathing and circulation.
The Circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of the brain.
The left anterior descending artery supplies much of the front of the left ventricle and the septum.
The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two, with the lingula part of the upper lobe.
A quick list on diaphragm openings: Vena cava passes at about T8; Oesophagus passes at about T10.
The liver is divided into eight segments, each with its own blood supply and drainage, which lets surgeons remove parts of it.
When the liver is diseased, pressure in the portal vein rises.
The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum at about T12 to L3.
The spleen lies under the left ribs, roughly ribs 9 to 11.
The radial nerve winds around the shaft of the humerus.
A quick list on layers of the skin: Epidermis: the outer protective layer; Dermis: contains collagen, vessels, nerves and glands.
A quick list on stages of anaesthesia: Stage 1: analgesia; Stage 2: excitement, with the risk of laryngospasm and vomiting.
MAC is the concentration of a gas at which half of patients do not move in response to a surgical incision.
A quick list on rapid sequence induction: Pre-oxygenate the patient; Give the induction drug and a fast-acting relaxant together.
The Mallampati score grades how much of the throat can be seen with the mouth open (class I to IV).
A quick list on safe extubation: The patient is awake or deeply anaesthetised by plan; Obeying commands and breathing well.
When nitrous oxide is turned off, it rushes out of the blood into the lungs and dilutes the oxygen there.
Awareness means a patient remembers being awake during surgery.
In TIVA, drugs such as propofol are given by infusion, often with a pump, instead of using inhaled gas.
A quick list on anaesthetic machine checks: Check gas supplies and the backup cylinder; Perform a leak test of the breathing circuit.
Breathing 100 percent oxygen through a tight-fitting mask for about three minutes of quiet breathing, or eight deep breaths, fills the lungs with oxygen.
A quick list on halsted's principles: Gentle handling of tissue; Careful haemostasis.
A quick list on wound healing by intention: Primary: wound edges are closed and heal directly; Secondary: wound is left open and fills in from the base.
Dead space is an empty pocket left in tissues.
Dead tissue and pus must be removed because antibiotics cannot reach them.
In a very sick or unstable patient, damage control surgery stops bleeding and contamination quickly, leaves the abdomen temporarily open and sends the patient for resu...
A quick list on ways to stop bleeding: Direct pressure and packing; Ligatures, clips and sutures.
Skin edges should meet gently, slightly everted, without tight sutures.
Drains stay until the output is low, usually small daily volumes, and the fluid looks right.
A quick list on asa physical status: I: healthy patient; II: mild systemic disease.
A quick list on enhanced recovery (eras): Good information and preparation before surgery; Short fasting and carbohydrate drinks where allowed.
A quick list on the primary survey: x: catastrophic bleeding first, where relevant; A: airway with neck protection.
The GCS adds three scores: eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and motor response (1 to 6).
Tension pneumothorax: air trapped under pressure.
FAST looks for free fluid (usually blood) in four places: around the heart, around the liver, around the spleen and in the pelvis.
Severe pelvic fractures can bleed heavily.
Rising pressure inside the skull can cause high blood pressure, a slow heart rate and irregular breathing.
A quick list on rule of nines for burns: Head and neck: 9 percent; Each arm: 9 percent.
Do not remove an object that is stuck in the body outside the operating theatre.
Tetanus-prone wounds include dirty, deep, crushed or old wounds.
Crushed muscle releases myoglobin and potassium.
The 4-2-1 rule gives maintenance fluid per hour: 4 mL per kg for the first 10 kg, 2 mL per kg for the next 10 kg and 1 mL per kg for the rest.
Sodium below about 135 mmol/L.
A quick list on treating high potassium: Protect the heart with calcium; Shift potassium into cells with insulin and glucose, and salbutamol.
Low potassium causes weakness and heart rhythm problems.
Low calcium can follow thyroid or parathyroid surgery and massive blood transfusion (citrate binds calcium).
Low magnesium can cause muscle twitching, low potassium and dangerous rhythms such as torsades de pointes.
A quick list on signs of dehydration: Dry mouth and reduced skin elasticity; Fast heart rate and low blood pressure.
A quick list on signs of fluid overload: Crackles in the lungs and breathlessness; Swollen legs or puffy eyelids.
After a long period of starvation, restarting feeding causes a shift in phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells.
Dextrose solutions provide sugar and free water.
X-rays pass through the body.
CT uses many X-ray images to build slices of the body.
MRI uses a strong magnet.
Reactions range from nausea and a rash to severe anaphylactoid reactions.
Higher frequency sound waves give sharper images but do not travel as far.
A quick list on reading a normal ecg: P wave: atrial activity; QRS complex: ventricular contraction.
An endotracheal tube tip should lie about 2 to 4 cm above the carina.
Reduce radiation by limiting time, increasing distance and using shielding.
An echocardiogram shows heart size, valve function and pumping.
If bowel perforation is suspected, water-soluble contrast is used rather than barium.
A quick list on the who analgesic ladder: Step 1: non-opioids such as paracetamol and NSAIDs; Step 2: weak opioids such as codeine.
The usual adult maximum is 4 g in 24 hours, with doses of 1 g at least 4 hours apart.
NSAIDs can cause stomach bleeding, kidney injury, raised blood pressure and reduce platelet function.
A PCA pump lets the patient give themselves a small dose of opioid by pressing a button.
Increasing sleepiness often appears before breathing slows.
Burning, shooting or electric pain suggests nerve damage.
Many patients feel pain, burning or cramps in a limb that has been removed.
People who take opioids regularly are often tolerant and may need higher doses for pain.
A quick list on epidural analgesia monitoring: Check pain scores and sensory level; Watch blood pressure, heart rate and leg weakness.

items.t: Pain in people who cannot speak
items.c: Patients with dementia or learning disability may show pain through facial expression, sounds, restlessness or changes in behaviour.
The A0 value measures the heat killing effect.
Enzymatic detergents break down blood, proteins and tissue on instruments.
Cannulated and tubular instruments hold blood and debris inside.

Many guidelines limit instrument set weight to around 10 kg (about 25 lb) so they dry properly and are safe to lift.
Peel pouches, wraps and rigid containers each have a role.
Sets from suppliers arrive unsterile or of unknown status.
Records link each sterilised set to the load, date and, where possible, the patient.
Ethylene oxide leaves residue in plastics and rubber.
Hard tap water leaves spots and deposits on instruments.
James Reason's model compares safety barriers to slices of Swiss cheese.
A quick list on human factors: Fatigue and stress reduce performance; Interruptions cause omissions.
A quick list on closed-loop communication: Give a clear instruction with the person's name; The receiver repeats it back.
Situation awareness means noticing what is happening, understanding it and predicting what is next.

Checklists catch simple, easily forgotten steps in complex work.
A pre-list briefing shares the plan, equipment, risks and roles.

items.t: Skin and positioning in the elderly
items.c: Older skin is thin and tears easily.
Older patients lose heat faster and recover from cold more slowly.
Hip fracture patients are often frail and in pain.
Dementia does not automatically mean a patient lacks capacity.
Older patients are at risk after sedation, with low blood pressure, weakness and unfamiliar rooms.

items.c: Older patients become dehydrated quickly.

Start simple pain relief before the block or anaesthetic wears off.

Place your fingers behind the angles of the jaw and lift it forward.

Group instruments by use: cutting, clamping, holding, retracting and suction.

Delicate work uses fine forceps, dissectors, bipolar diathermy and self-retaining retainers.

A flap moves tissue with its own blood supply attached.
Superficial burns are red and painful.

Hands are complex, with tendons, nerves and fine blood vessels.
A tourniquet gives a dry field in limb surgery.

Inhaled objects, especially in small children, can cause sudden coughing, wheeze or noisy breathing.

Nasal packs or balloons compress bleeding vessels.

Glaucoma damages the optic nerve, often with raised eye pressure.
Many eye operations use topical drops or a local anaesthetic block, with the patient awake.
Fine eye surgery is done under a microscope.

The retina can peel away from the back of the eye.
If an eye injury may have punctured the globe, do not press on it.

Third molars may lack room and stay partly under the gum.

Children have faster heart and breathing rates, smaller airways and less energy reserve.

If a testis has not come down to the scrotum, surgery is usually done in infancy to bring it down.
One part of bowel slides into another.
Both are birth defects where bowel and organs lie outside the abdomen.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart under higher pressure and have thick, muscular walls.

items.t: The six Ps of acute limb ischaemia
items.c: A quick list on the six ps of acute limb ischaemia: Pain, pallor, pulselessness; Paraesthesia, paralysis.
A balloon catheter can be passed beyond a clot in an artery, inflated, and pulled back to remove the clot.
