A stoma changes body image and daily life.
Appendicitis often starts with pain around the belly button that moves to the lower right abdomen, with nausea and fever.
Signs are colicky pain, vomiting, a swollen abdomen and no passage of stool or gas.
The sigmoid colon can twist on its mesentery, especially in older people, causing a massively swollen abdomen and constipation.
Peritonitis is inflammation of the abdominal lining, often from a burst bowel or appendix.
In an unconscious patient the tongue and soft tissues fall back and block the throat.
An oropharyngeal airway holds the tongue forward in an unconscious patient.
A nasopharyngeal airway is better tolerated by lightly anaesthetised or semi-conscious patients.
A laryngeal mask sits over the larynx and seals around it.
A quick list on preparing for intubation: soapme: S - Suction ready and working; O - Oxygen source and mask.
For intubation the head is usually raised on a pillow or ring and the neck flexed, with the head extended at the top.
A quick list on confirming tube position: Look: chest rises on both sides; Listen: breath sounds equal, none over stomach.
A tracheal tube cuff seals the airway and protects against leaks.
Extubation is usually done when the patient is awake, breathing well, obeying commands and protecting the airway.
A quick list on recognising a blocked airway: Snoring means a partial blockage; Gurgling means fluid in the airway.
Pulse oximetry shows oxygen saturation of haemoglobin, not ventilation.
The capnograph shows carbon dioxide in each breath.
Theatre ECG shows heart rate and rhythm.
The blood pressure cuff bladder should cover about two thirds of the upper arm length and wrap around most of its circumference.
Anaesthesia impairs temperature control, so patients often become cold.
Urine output reflects blood flow to the kidneys and gives a clue to fluid status.
A quick list on minimum monitoring standard: Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry; Blood pressure at regular intervals.
Processed EEG monitors such as BIS give a number linked to how deeply the brain is anaesthetised.
A nerve stimulator on a peripheral nerve checks how much a muscle relaxant is working.
A quick list on alarms: set and respect: Set limits suitable for this patient; Never switch alarms off for convenience.
In spontaneous ventilation the patient draws air by negative chest pressure.
Tidal volume is usually set by ideal body weight, not actual weight.
PEEP keeps some pressure in the airways at the end of each breath.
Use a C-grip on the mask with thumb and index finger, and lift the jaw with the remaining fingers.
A rising peak airway pressure suggests a problem such as a kinked tube, bronchospasm, secretions, a tube in one lung, or the patient coughing or straining.
A quick list on causes of hypoxia under ga: Equipment: no oxygen, disconnection, blocked tube; Airway: obstruction, laryngospasm, oesophageal tube.
Atelectasis is collapse of small areas of lung.
In some chest operations one lung is deflated so the surgeon can work.
A quick list on weaning from the ventilator: Patient warm and reasonably pain controlled; Muscle relaxant worn off or reversed.
Hypoventilation raises carbon dioxide, causing drowsiness, a fast pulse and, when severe, acidosis.
Post-operative nausea and vomiting is more likely in women, non-smokers, those with a past history or motion sickness, and after long surgery or opioids.
Laryngospasm is a forceful closure of the vocal cords, often at light anaesthesia from secretions, blood or stimulation.
Bronchospasm is narrowing of the small airways.
Aspiration happens when stomach contents enter the lungs, usually when airway reflexes are lost.
A quick list on anaphylaxis in theatre: Sudden fall in blood pressure or collapse; Bronchospasm, rash or swelling of the face.
Awareness means the patient recalls events during surgery.
Sore throat is common after intubation or a laryngeal mask.
Teeth can be damaged by laryngoscopy, especially if loose or capped.
Nerves can be stretched or compressed when patients are anaesthetised.
A quick list on hypotension under anaesthesia: Common causes: anaesthetic drugs, low volume; Bleeding, regional block, or sepsis.
In pregnancy the airway is swollen, oxygen consumption rises, and the lungs have less reserve.
Lying flat late in pregnancy, the uterus can press on the vena cava and reduce blood return to the heart.
Spinal anaesthesia is often preferred for caesarean section.
Airway swelling, large breasts and weight gain can make intubation harder in pregnancy.
Pregnant women are treated as having a full stomach from mid pregnancy onward, especially in labour.
An epidural places a thin catheter near the spinal nerves so local anaesthetic can be given gradually.
A quick list on post-partum haemorrhage: Think the four Ts: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin; Call for help early and start two large drips.
Pre-eclampsia involves raised blood pressure, protein in the urine and possible organ involvement.
Drugs given to the mother can cross the placenta and affect the baby.
After delivery, oxytocin helps the uterus contract and reduces bleeding.
A quick list on the anaesthetic history: Past anaesthetics and any problems; Family history of anaesthetic reactions.
The ASA score groups patients from healthy (class 1) to brain dead (class 6).
The patient sits, opens wide and sticks out the tongue without saying a sound.
A quick list on other airway tests: Mouth opening: can three fingers fit?; Thyromental distance: space under the chin.
Fasting reduces the risk of aspiration.
Asking about daily activity helps predict risk.
Some drugs are usually continued, such as many heart and asthma medicines.
The patient should understand the anaesthetic plan, main risks, alternatives and what to expect after.
Anaemia reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood and increases the need for transfusion.
A quick list on pre-operative checklist: Right patient, procedure and site; Consent signed and fasting confirmed.
A quick list on sedation levels: Minimal: calm, responds normally to voice; Moderate: responds purposefully to touch or voice.
Midazolam gives anxiety relief, sedation and memory loss and is short acting.
Propofol acts quickly and wears off quickly, but the line between sedation and general anaesthesia is thin.
Ketamine produces a trance-like state with strong pain relief, while airway reflexes and breathing are often better preserved.
Sedation can lower airway protection even if the patient seems awake.
A quick list on monitoring sedated patients: Continuous pulse oximetry; Capnography where available.
Children have less oxygen reserve, smaller airways and fast metabolism.
Opioids and sedatives each depress breathing and together the effect is more than doubled.
Naloxone reverses opioid effect and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
A patient is ready to go home when awake, oriented, breathing and moving normally, and with stable observations.
Oxygen supports life and nitrous oxide gives analgesia and mild anaesthesia.
A quick list on gas cylinder colours: Oxygen: white shoulders, black body (common); Nitrous oxide: blue.
Cylinder yokes have pins in set positions, and each cylinder has matching holes.
Sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane and halothane are examples of volatile agents.
MAC is the minimum alveolar concentration of an agent that prevents movement in half of patients in response to a surgical stimulus.
A quick list on vaporiser safety: Fill only with the agent named on the vaporiser; Use the correct, keyed filling system.
In circle systems, soda lime absorbs the carbon dioxide patients breathe out so gases can be reused.
When nitrous oxide is switched off, it moves rapidly from blood into the lungs and can dilute the oxygen there.
Anaesthetic gases leaking into theatre can be breathed by staff.
Some anaesthetic gases are strong greenhouse gases, and desflurane and nitrous oxide have a larger impact than most others.
Oxygen is given to prevent or treat low blood oxygen.
Nasal cannulae are comfortable and allow eating and talking.
A simple face mask delivers a moderate oxygen concentration and needs a minimum flow to wash out exhaled carbon dioxide.
A mask with a reservoir bag and one-way valves delivers high oxygen concentrations.
A Venturi mask delivers a fixed oxygen percentage using colour-coded valves and a set flow.
In some people with chronic lung disease, too much oxygen can cause carbon dioxide retention and drowsiness.
An oxygen concentrator takes in room air, removes most nitrogen and delivers oxygen-enriched air.
A quick list on oxygen cylinder safety: Keep cylinders upright and secured; No oil, grease or open flames nearby.
Dry oxygen can dry and irritate airways, thicken secretions and make patients uncomfortable.
A quick list on signs oxygen is not enough: Rising breathing rate and effort; Confusion, restlessness or drowsiness.
Malignant hyperthermia is an inherited reaction to some volatile agents and suxamethonium.
Too much local anaesthetic in the blood, or an accidental injection into a vein, can cause tingling around the mouth, seizures, collapse and cardiac arrest.
A total spinal happens when local anaesthetic spreads too high in the spinal fluid.
Some people break down suxamethonium slowly because of a genetic enzyme variation.
Air trapped in the chest can push the lung and heart to one side.
Air can enter veins during neurosurgery, laparoscopy or central line work.
When cement is placed in the bone during some orthopaedic operations, some patients develop low oxygen, low blood pressure or cardiac arrest.
If tracheal intubation fails and the patient cannot be oxygenated by mask or supraglottic device, a front-of-neck access procedure may be needed.
A quick list on intraoperative cardiac arrest: Call for help and start chest compressions; Check rhythm and treat per protocol.
A transfusion reaction may show as fever, rash, breathlessness, back pain or low blood pressure.
A general abdominal set usually holds scalpel handles, scissors, tissue and dissecting forceps, many artery forceps, needle holders, retractors and towel clips.
A quick list on counting instruments in a set: Count at set-up, before closure and at the end; Two people count aloud and both agree.
A quick list on instrument classes by function: Cutting: scalpels, scissors, osteotomes; Grasping: tissue and dissecting forceps.
Artery forceps have serrated jaws and a ratchet that locks the handles shut.
Hand-held retractors, such as Langenbeck or Deaver types, are held by an assistant.
A needle holder grips the curved needle near its back third.
Toothed forceps grip tough tissue such as skin and fascia with little pressure.
A caesarean set usually includes scalpel handles, scissors, forceps, artery forceps, retractors such as a bladder blade, needle holders and cord clamps.
Orthopaedic sets contain heavy items such as mallets, osteotomes, drills, reamers and bone levers.
A quick list on setting up the mayo stand: Place sharps and most-used items within reach; Arrange instruments in the order of use.
Rigid endoscopes, such as laparoscopes and cystoscopes, are metal tubes with lens systems.
The light source sends bright light along a fibre-optic cable to the scope.
The camera head attaches to the eyepiece and sends the picture to the monitor.
The insufflator delivers carbon dioxide into the abdomen to lift the wall and create working space.
A trocar with a sleeve (cannula) is used to make an access port for instruments.
A quick list on basic video tower layout: Monitor placed in the surgeon's line of sight; Light source, camera unit and insufflator on tower.
The lens system inside a rigid telescope is delicate.
A leak test pressurises the scope to check that the outer covering is intact.
A quick list on cleaning a flexible scope: Wipe and flush channels straight after use; Leak test before immersion.
Procedures such as cystoscopy or hysteroscopy use fluid to expand the space and clear the view.
A quick list on zoning of the theatre suite: Outer zone: reception, changing, store; Clean zone: pre-op area and clean corridors.
In many theatres, air pressure inside is slightly higher than in the corridor.
Theatres need many air changes per hour to dilute airborne microbes.
Each opening of the door and each person in the room raises the number of microbes in the air.
Floors, walls and ceilings in theatre should be smooth, seamless, non-porous and able to withstand frequent cleaning and disinfectants.
The scrub area has deep sinks with elbow, knee, foot or sensor taps so hands are not used to turn water on or off.
Theatre temperature is set to balance staff comfort with patient warmth, and it often differs for babies and burns patients, who need warmer rooms.
Many theatres have wall or pendant outlets for oxygen, medical air, suction and sometimes nitrous oxide.
Theatre needs electricity for lights, anaesthesia machines, suction and monitors.
A quick list on clean and dirty flow: Sterile supplies enter through the clean route; Patient enters through the reception route.
A quick list on cssd one-way workflow: Receive used items in the dirty area; Clean and decontaminate.
Blood and tissue left on instruments protect microbes from steam and chemicals.
Staff handle sharps, so wear gloves, a plastic apron and eye protection.
An ultrasonic cleaner uses high-frequency sound in liquid to loosen dirt from joints, serrations and hollow parts.
Sets are packed so that steam can reach all surfaces.
A quick list on steam sterilisation cycle: Air is removed from the chamber; Steam enters and heats the load.
Chemical indicators change colour when conditions are met, such as on tape or strips inside packs.
Leave space between packs so steam can circulate.
Sterile items are stored in clean, dry, closed shelves or cupboards away from sinks, dust and direct sunlight.
Each autoclave load gets a record of the machine, cycle, date and contents.
Reusable cloth drapes are washed, checked and sterilised after each use.
Standard gowns protect the surgical team from moderate splashes.
On a sterile gown, the front from chest to waist level and the sleeves up to the elbows are regarded as sterile.
A quick list on steps for gowning: Open the pack without touching the gown; Lift it by the inside neckline.
In closed gloving, hands remain inside the gown cuffs while pulling the glove on.
A quick list on draping the surgical site: Drape only after skin preparation has dried; Place drapes from the clean area outwards.
A fenestrated drape has an opening (a fenestration) to expose only the operating site.
Some operations use a clear adhesive film over the prepared skin so the incision goes through it.
When fluid soaks through a drape or gown, microbes can travel from the unsterile layer to the sterile surface.
A quick list on drape and gown packaging checks: Check pack is intact and not damp; Check indicator has changed colour.
Most surgical needles are curved so they can turn through tissue.
Absorbable sutures are broken down by the body over time and are used for internal tissue.
A quick list on reading suture packets: Material, such as silk, nylon or polyglactin; Size number, with more zeros meaning finer.
Swabs used inside body cavities should have an X-ray detectable marker so a retained item can be found by imaging.
Skin staplers place metal staples quickly and are common in long wounds.
A drain removes blood or fluid that could collect after surgery.
A wound dressing protects the wound, absorbs fluid and keeps it clean.
Haemostatic products, such as absorbable gelatin sponges or cellulose-based materials, help control oozing from raw surfaces.
A urinary catheter drains the bladder and measures urine output in long or major surgery.
A quick list on stock rotation and expiry: Place new stock behind older stock; Use items with the earliest expiry first.
Preventive maintenance is planned servicing done on a schedule to stop breakdowns.
A quick list on daily equipment checks: Check power cables and plugs for damage; Switch on and test alarms.
Each major item should have a record of its serial number, service dates, repairs and faults.
Surfaces that staff and patients touch, such as tables, light handles, monitors, trolleys and pendants, are wiped down with a suitable disinfectant between cases.
If equipment behaves oddly, stop using it if safe to do so, tell the team and report it as per local policy.
A faulty item should be clearly tagged "out of service" and moved away from working equipment.
Many theatre devices rely on batteries as backup, such as monitors, laryngoscopes and suction units.
A quick list on inspecting cables and plugs: Look for cuts, kinks or exposed wire; Check plug pins for bending or burn marks.
Calibration compares a device with a known standard and adjusts it so readings are accurate.
Autoclaves need regular checks such as cleaning the chamber and drain, checking door seals and gauges, and servicing by qualified staff.
An operating table usually has a top that is divided into head, back, seat and leg sections.
Before moving a patient onto the table, make sure the brakes or locking mechanism are on and the table is at a safe height.
A quick list on safe patient transfer: Check table and trolley brakes are on; Use enough staff and a slide sheet or board.
Positioning aids include arm boards, gel pads, head rings, side supports, leg holders and foot boards.
In lithotomy, the legs are raised in supports for gynaecological, urological and some rectal surgery.
The prone position places the patient on the stomach, usually after anaesthesia.
In the lateral position, the patient lies on one side, often for kidney or chest operations.
Trendelenburg tilts the patient head-down.
Theatre lights give bright, white, shadow-free light on the surgical site.
A quick list on handling and positioning lights: Use the sterile handle or cover as directed; Move slowly to avoid bumping heads.
An implant is a device placed inside the body, often for a long time, such as a screw or mesh.
Implants are often made from stainless steel, titanium, special plastics or ceramics.
Plates and screws hold fractured bone in position while it heals.
An intramedullary nail is a rod passed down the hollow centre of a long bone, such as the femur or tibia, to hold a fracture.
Hip and knee replacements use several parts that must fit together, such as a stem, a head and a socket for the hip.
A quick list on handling sterile implants: Open only when the surgeon asks for it; Check name, size, side and expiry.
A quick list on implant records and traceability: Record the type, size and batch number; Store the sticker or label in the notes.
A surgical mesh is a net-like implant placed to strengthen a weak area, such as in hernia repair.
Bone cement is mixed from a powder and a liquid in theatre.
Patients may have implanted devices such as pacemakers, which can be affected by diathermy current.
Biomedical engineers install, test, maintain and repair medical equipment.
Earthing gives stray electrical current a safe path to the ground, so it does not pass through a person.
All electrical equipment has a tiny leakage current.
A pulse oximeter shines two types of light through tissue, usually a finger or ear.
Diathermy passes high-frequency current through tissue to cut or coagulate.
A quick list on suction unit basics: Collection jar to hold fluid; Tubing linking patient to jar.
A defibrillator delivers a controlled electric shock to treat certain life-threatening heart rhythms.
A voltage stabiliser smooths out highs and lows in the mains supply.
A pneumatic tourniquet uses an inflatable cuff and a pressure controller to stop blood flowing into a limb during surgery.
A quick list on layers of the scalp: S - Skin; C - Connective tissue (dense, holds vessels).

items.t: Why scalp wounds bleed so much
items.c: Scalp arteries run in the dense connective layer, which holds cut vessels open, so even small wounds bleed heavily.
The facial nerve runs through the parotid gland and fans out into branches that move the face.
The sternocleidomastoid muscle splits each side of the neck into an anterior and a posterior triangle.
The accessory nerve (XI) runs superficially in the posterior triangle and supplies trapezius.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the thyroid blood vessels and supplies most laryngeal muscles.
There are usually four small parathyroid glands behind the thyroid.
A quick list on cartilages of the larynx: Thyroid - largest, forms the Adam's apple; Cricoid - only complete ring, below thyroid.
This membrane lies between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, just below the vocal cords, and is thin and near the skin.
A quick list on contents of the carotid sheath: Common and internal carotid artery (medial); Internal jugular vein (lateral).
Each intercostal space has a vein, artery and nerve (VAN) running in a groove under the lower edge of the rib above.
The triangle of safety lies on the side of the chest.
The pleura covers the lung and lines the chest wall.

items.t: Lobes and fissures of the lungs
items.c: A quick list on lobes and fissures of the lungs: Right lung: three lobes (upper, middle, lower); Right fissures: oblique and horizontal.
The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.
A quick list on diaphragm hiatuses by level: T8 - vena cava (I Eight Ten Eggs Aorta Twelve); T10 - oesophagus and vagus nerves.
The phrenic nerve comes from roots C3 to C5 and is the main nerve to the diaphragm.
A quick list on blood flow through the heart: Body to right atrium via vena cavae; Right atrium - tricuspid - right ventricle.
The coronary arteries arise from the aortic root just above the aortic valve.
The mediastinum sits between the lungs.
A quick list on layers in a midline incision: Skin; Subcutaneous fat and Scarpa's fascia.
The rectus abdominis muscle is wrapped in a sheath formed by flat muscle aponeuroses.
The inguinal canal is an oblique passage about 4 cm long above the inguinal ligament.
Indirect hernias pass through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
The peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity and covers organs.
A quick list on gut blood supply by region: Coeliac trunk - foregut (stomach, liver, spleen); SMA - midgut (small bowel, right colon).
Calot's triangle is bordered by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct and liver edge.
A quick list on bile duct pathway: Right and left hepatic ducts leave the liver; Join as the common hepatic duct.
The appendix base lies at the point where the three taenia coli of the caecum meet.
The spleen sits under the left ribs, roughly ribs 9 to 11, and is soft and rich in blood.

items.t: Bones and joints of the pelvis
items.c: The pelvis is formed by two hip bones, the sacrum and the coccyx.
Levator ani and related muscles form a sling that supports the bladder, uterus or prostate, and rectum.
A quick list on female pelvic organs: Bladder lies in front; Uterus sits in the middle, with the cervix below.
In the pelvis, the ureter passes close to and beneath the uterine artery, like water under a bridge.
The uterine artery comes from the internal iliac artery and joins branches from the ovarian artery.
The prostate surrounds the first part of the urethra just below the bladder.
An empty bladder sits behind the pubic bones; when full it rises into the abdomen.
The pudendal nerve comes from sacral roots S2 to S4 and supplies the perineum and part of the pelvic floor.
A quick list on rectum and anal canal: Rectum follows the curve of the sacrum; Anal canal is the last part, about 4 cm.
A quick list on pelvic inlet and outlet: Inlet (brim) - top opening of the true pelvis; Cavity - the canal between inlet and outlet.
A quick list on brachial plexus layout: Roots - C5 to T1; Trunks - upper, middle, lower.
The brachial plexus leaves the neck between the anterior and middle scalene muscles and passes above the first rib and under the collarbone.
The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and supplies the deltoid and a patch of skin over the shoulder.
The radial nerve spirals around the humerus in the spiral groove and supplies the muscles that extend the wrist and fingers.
The median nerve passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist and supplies the thumb side of the hand and the muscles of the thumb base.

items.t: Ulnar nerve and the funny bone
items.c: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, close to the skin, where a bump causes a sharp tingle.
A quick list on cubital fossa contents: Triangle in front of the elbow; Medial to lateral: median nerve, brachial artery.
Both arteries supply the hand through arches in the palm.
A quick list on rotator cuff muscles: Supraspinatus - starts arm abduction; Infraspinatus - rotates arm outward.
The cephalic vein runs on the thumb side and the basilic vein on the little finger side.
A quick list on femoral triangle contents: Edges: inguinal ligament, sartorius, adductor; Contents from lateral to medial:.
The femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point, halfway between the front hip bone and the pubic bone.
The sciatic nerve, made of roots L4 to S3, leaves the pelvis below the piriformis muscle and runs down the back of the thigh.
Intramuscular buttock injections go into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock, away from the sciatic nerve, which lies in the lower inner part.
The common peroneal nerve winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin and is easily pressed.
The femoral nerve arises from L2 to L4 and supplies the quadriceps muscle and skin of the front of the thigh.
The great saphenous vein runs up the inner leg from in front of the ankle's inner bone to the groin, where it joins the femoral vein.
A quick list on popliteal fossa: Diamond space behind the knee; Tibial nerve - most superficial.
A quick list on compartments of the leg: Anterior - lifts the foot; Lateral - turns the foot outward.
A thigh tourniquet uses a wide cuff over padding at the upper thigh.
A quick list on regions of the vertebral column: Cervical - 7 vertebrae in the neck; Thoracic - 12 with ribs attached.
A typical vertebra has a body in front for weight bearing, and an arch behind made of pedicles and laminae.
The atlas (C1) has no body and holds the skull; nodding mainly happens at this joint.
A disc has a soft core, the nucleus pulposus, inside a tough ring, the annulus fibrosus.
In adults the spinal cord usually ends around L1 to L2, and in young children a little lower.

items.t: Layers crossed by a spinal needle
items.c: A quick list on layers crossed by a spinal needle: Skin and subcutaneous tissue; Supraspinous then interspinous ligament.
A line between the highest points of the iliac crests usually crosses around L4 or the L4-5 space.
The epidural space lies between the dura and the bony canal, containing fat, veins and nerve roots.
The spine has four curves.
The spine can be thought of as anterior, middle and posterior columns.
The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord.
A quick list on the three meninges: Dura mater - tough outer layer; Arachnoid mater - thin middle web.
CSF is made mostly in the choroid plexus of the brain ventricles.
The circle of Willis is a ring of arteries at the base of the brain fed by the internal carotids and the basilar artery.
A quick list on sympathetic and parasympathetic: Sympathetic: fight or flight; Faster heart rate, wider pupils, raised pressure.
A reflex arc has a sensor, a sensory nerve, a relay in the spinal cord or brainstem, a motor nerve and a muscle or gland.
Nerve signals travel along axons, and myelin speeds them up.
A quick list on glasgow coma scale parts: Eye opening (E); Verbal response (V).
The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) supplies the throat, heart, lungs and gut.
Bones are grouped by shape: long (femur), short (wrist and ankle bones), flat (skull, ribs, sternum), irregular (vertebrae) and sesamoid (the patella, set in a tendon).
Hard compact bone forms the outer shell.
A broken bone first forms a haematoma.
Healing needs blood supply, stability and good nutrition.
A quick list on features of a synovial joint: Articular cartilage covers bone ends; Joint capsule surrounds the joint.
Hinge joints, like the elbow, bend one way.
The hip is a deep ball and socket joint.
The anterior cruciate ligament stops the shin sliding forward and the posterior cruciate stops it sliding back.
In children the growth plate, or physis, is weaker than nearby ligaments, so injuries often break the plate rather than tear a ligament.
Osteoporosis makes bones lose density and become brittle, mostly in older people, especially after menopause.
A quick list on layers of the eye: Outer - sclera (white) and cornea (clear front); Middle - choroid, ciliary body and iris.
The iris muscles change pupil size.
The ciliary body makes aqueous humour, which drains at the angle between iris and cornea.
The cornea has no blood vessels and is very sensitive.
The retina has rods, which see in dim light, and cones, which see colour and detail.
The outer ear collects sound to the eardrum.
The Eustachian tube links the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure either side of the eardrum.
The semicircular canals and vestibule detect head movement.
Skin has receptors for light touch, pressure, vibration, warmth, cold and pain.
Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps each minute.
A quick list on determinants of stroke volume: Preload: how full the ventricle is before beating; Contractility: the strength of the squeeze.
Within limits, the more the heart muscle is stretched by filling, the harder it contracts.
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is the average pressure driving blood through organs.
Stretch sensors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect blood pressure.
A quick list on cardiac conduction pathway: Sinoatrial node starts the impulse; Atrioventricular node delays it briefly.
The P wave shows atrial depolarisation.

items.t: Venous return and the muscle pump
items.c: Veins have valves, and contracting leg muscles squeeze blood towards the heart.
Most blood flow to the left ventricle occurs during diastole, when the muscle relaxes and vessels are not squeezed.
A quick list on compensation in blood loss: Heart rate rises first; Vessels constrict to protect core organs.
Tidal volume is the air moved in one normal breath.
FRC is the air left in the lungs after a normal breath out.
Efficient gas exchange needs air and blood in the same place.
The curve shows how haemoglobin binds oxygen at different pressures.
Breathing is set by respiratory centres in the brainstem.
A quick list on work of breathing signs: Nasal flaring and tracheal tug; Intercostal and subcostal recession.
Surfactant lowers surface tension inside alveoli and stops them collapsing at the end of a breath.
Small areas of lung can collapse soon after induction, especially in the dependent parts, after high oxygen concentrations, or from reduced FRC.
Hypoxaemia means low oxygen in the blood.
A quick list on causes of hypoxaemia: Low inspired oxygen; Hypoventilation.
Each nephron has a glomerulus that filters blood, and tubules that reabsorb useful substances and secrete waste.
GFR is the volume of blood filtered by the kidneys each minute.
Healthy kidneys keep blood flow and filtration fairly constant across a wide range of blood pressures.
A quick list on renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system: Low pressure or low sodium triggers renin release; Renin leads to angiotensin II formation.
ADH is released by the pituitary when blood is concentrated or volume is low.
The kidneys excrete hydrogen ions and regulate bicarbonate.
Most potassium is inside cells, and the kidneys control how much is lost.
A quick list on nephrotoxic risks to remember: Some antibiotics, such as aminoglycosides; Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
The kidneys make erythropoietin, which signals bone marrow to produce red cells when oxygen delivery is low.
A quick list on liver functions overview: Makes clotting factors and albumin; Metabolises many drugs.
The liver receives blood from the hepatic artery, which carries oxygen, and from the portal vein, which carries nutrients from the gut.
Drugs absorbed from the gut pass through the liver before reaching general circulation.
Bile salts help break fats into small droplets so they can be digested and absorbed.
A quick list on bilirubin and jaundice: Pre-hepatic: too much red cell breakdown; Hepatic: liver cells cannot process bilirubin.
Surgery, opioids, electrolyte disturbance and handling of the bowel can slow or stop gut movement.
Anaesthesia removes protective airway reflexes, so stomach contents may travel into the lungs.
Liver failure lowers albumin and clotting factors.
A quick list on portal hypertension features: Raised pressure in the portal venous system; Oesophageal varices that may bleed.
After meals the liver stores glucose as glycogen.
A nerve impulse is a wave of sodium entering the cell, followed by potassium leaving.
At a synapse, a nerve releases a chemical messenger that binds to receptors on the next cell.
A quick list on sympathetic versus parasympathetic: Sympathetic: fight or flight; Raises heart rate and widens airways.
A quick list on pain pathway steps: Transduction: the stimulus is detected; Transmission: impulse travels to the spinal cord.
Brain blood flow is tightly controlled and is strongly affected by carbon dioxide.
The skull has a fixed volume containing brain, blood and cerebrospinal fluid.

items.t: Spinal cord levels and block height
items.c: Nerves leave the spinal cord at set levels.
A motor nerve releases acetylcholine, which binds receptors on muscle and triggers contraction.
General anaesthesia is a drug-induced state with loss of awareness, and is different from natural sleep.
A quick list on components of blood: Red cells carry oxygen; White cells fight infection.
Haemoglobin inside red cells carries most of the oxygen in blood.
A quick list on causes of anaemia: Iron deficiency: low iron, small pale cells; B12 or folate deficiency: large cells.
Sickle haemoglobin can distort red cells, blocking small vessels.
When a vessel is injured, it narrows and platelets stick to the exposed wall, then clump together to form a plug.
Clotting factors activate each other in sequence, finally turning fibrinogen into fibrin, which strengthens the platelet plug.
ABO groups depend on antigens on red cells.
A quick list on transfusion reaction signs: Fever or chills; Chest or back pain.
Fibrinolysis is the natural breakdown of clots.
A low platelet count raises the risk of bleeding, especially with surgery or injections near the spine.
Innate immunity is quick and general, and includes skin, mucus, phagocytes and inflammation.
Intact skin blocks most microbes.
A quick list on antibodies and their classes: IgG: most common, crosses the placenta; IgM: first to appear in infection.
A quick list on types of hypersensitivity: Type I: immediate, such as anaphylaxis; Type II: antibody attacks cells.
Anaphylaxis can cause low blood pressure, wheeze, swelling of the face or airway, rash and fast heart rate, often within minutes of exposure.
Latex allergy may be immediate or delayed.
A quick list on inflammation signs: Redness; Heat.
Steroids, chemotherapy, HIV and transplant drugs can weaken immune defences.
Active immunity develops when the body makes its own response, through infection or vaccination.
Complement proteins circulate in the blood and activate in sequence.
Cells may adapt, suffer reversible injury or die.
Necrosis is uncontrolled death from injury, often causing inflammation.
A quick list on phases of wound healing: Haemostasis: clotting stops bleeding; Inflammation: cells clear debris and germs.
A quick list on factors delaying healing: Infection; Poor blood supply.
Clots are more likely with slow blood flow, damaged vessel walls or blood that clots too easily.
An embolus is a mass that travels in the blood and blocks a vessel.
A quick list on benign versus malignant tumours: Benign: slow growth, usually stays local; Usually has a clear border.
A specimen must be labelled correctly with patient details and tissue site, placed in the right container, and sent with a complete request form.
A quick list on four types of shock: Hypovolaemic: lost blood or fluid; Cardiogenic: pump failure.
Oedema can come from raised vessel pressure, low albumin, leaky vessels or blocked lymph drainage.
Gram staining separates bacteria by cell wall structure.
A quick list on common surgical site pathogens: Staphylococcus aureus, often from skin; Coagulase-negative staphylococci.
Some bacteria, such as Clostridium and Bacillus, form spores that resist heat, drying and many disinfectants.
Tetanus bacteria live in soil and dung, and spores enter dirty wounds.
A quick list on blood-borne viruses: Hepatitis B; Hepatitis C.
After a sharps injury, wash the wound with soap and running water, do not squeeze or scrub hard, and report it right away.
Tuberculosis spreads through tiny droplets that stay in the air.
Bacteria can become resistant when antibiotics are overused or taken incompletely.
MRSA is a Staphylococcus aureus resistant to many common antibiotics.
Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by infection.
Plasmodium parasites enter through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito, multiply in the liver, then infect red cells and cause fever.
A quick list on severe malaria warning signs: Drowsiness or convulsions; Breathing difficulty.
Patients with active malaria may have anaemia, low platelets, low blood sugar and organ involvement.
Schistosomiasis is caught from freshwater containing larvae released by certain snails.
People can swallow eggs of Echinococcus tapeworms from dogs or contaminated food.
A quick list on soil-transmitted helminths: Roundworm (Ascaris); Hookworm.
Heavy roundworm infection, especially in children, can form a mass that blocks the bowel or bile ducts.
This parasite spreads through contaminated food and water.
Filarial worms live in lymph vessels and can cause chronic swelling of limbs or genitals.
A quick list on preventing parasitic infection: Safe drinking water; Handwashing and good sanitation.
Primary prevention stops disease before it starts, such as vaccination.
Incidence is the number of new cases in a set period.
When enough people are immune, the germ struggles to spread and some unprotected people are shielded.
A quick list on steps of an outbreak response: Confirm the cases and the diagnosis; Define a case and count cases by time, place, person.
Surveillance is the steady collection and review of health data so action can follow.
Most vaccines lose potency if too warm, and some are damaged by freezing.
Disease results from an agent (germ), a host (person) and an environment that brings them together.
Some diseases must be reported to health authorities as soon as they are suspected, for example cholera and measles.
A quick list on making household water safe: Collect from the cleanest source available; Filter out visible dirt through clean cloth.
A quick list on primary health care principles: Equity: care reaches everyone who needs it; Community participation in decisions.
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites passed on by bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, mostly at night.
A rapid diagnostic test detects malaria parasite proteins in a drop of blood and gives a result in minutes.
Typhoid spreads through food and water contaminated by faeces of an infected person.
Cholera causes sudden, profuse watery diarrhoea that can lead to dangerous dehydration within hours.
Spread by sandfly bites, kala-azar causes long fever, weight loss, a big spleen and anaemia.
A quick list on trachoma and the safe strategy: S: Surgery for in-turned eyelashes; A: Antibiotics for active infection.
Roundworm, whipworm and hookworm spread through soil contaminated by faeces.
Rabies spreads in the saliva of an infected animal, often a dog.
Current WHO advice is for pregnant women to have several antenatal contacts, starting early.
A quick list on danger signs in pregnancy: Vaginal bleeding; Severe headache or blurred vision.
Pre-eclampsia is high blood pressure with signs of organ strain, such as protein in urine, usually after 20 weeks.
The third stage runs from birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta.

items.t: The four Ts of postpartum bleeding
items.c: A quick list on the four ts of postpartum bleeding: Tone: the womb fails to contract; Trauma: tears of the birth canal or womb.
A partograph charts cervical opening, baby's heart rate, contractions, and maternal observations over time.
Mothers and babies need checks soon after birth and again within the first days and weeks.
Anaemia is common in pregnancy and raises risks of bleeding, infection and early birth.
A quick list on birth preparedness plan: Choose a skilled birth attendant and facility; Save money for transport and costs.
Counselling should give clear, unbiased information about methods, how well they work, side effects and who they suit.
Children receive scheduled vaccines from birth, with doses at set ages, against diseases such as tuberculosis, polio, measles, diphtheria, tetanus and whooping cough.
A quick list on imci general danger signs: Unable to drink or breastfeed; Vomits everything.
Plotting weight against age on a growth chart over time matters more than one reading.
Small babies are held upright against the mother's bare chest, wrapped, with frequent breastfeeding.
WHO advises breast milk alone, with no water or other foods, for about the first six months, then continued breastfeeding with other foods.
Oral rehydration solution replaces water and salts lost in diarrhoea.
In children with cough, fast breathing for their age is a key sign of pneumonia.
A quick list on newborn danger signs: Not feeding well or feeding poorly; Fits, floppy or very sleepy.
Some young children have a seizure with a high temperature.
Children usually learn to smile, sit, walk and talk in a broad but predictable order.
After infection, tests may not yet detect HIV.
HIV testing is voluntary, with pre-test information, informed consent and confidentiality.
People on effective antiretroviral therapy with a sustained undetectable viral load do not pass HIV on through sex.
Without intervention, HIV can pass during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.
After a needlestick or other high-risk exposure, antiretroviral drugs can lower infection risk if started quickly, ideally within hours and no later than around 72 hours.
HIV damages CD4 cells, so the body fails to resist infections such as TB, thrush and pneumonia.
A quick list on supporting adherence: Link pills to a daily routine; Use reminders, such as alarms or a buddy.
Viral load measures how much HIV is in the blood.
Fear of judgement keeps people from testing and treatment.
A quick list on after a sharps injury: Let the wound bleed gently, do not squeeze hard; Wash with soap and running water.
Pulmonary TB spreads when a person with active disease coughs, sneezes or speaks, releasing tiny droplets carrying Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
A quick list on tb symptom screening: Cough, especially lasting two weeks or more; Fever or night sweats.
GeneXpert is a molecular test that detects TB germs in sputum within hours and also shows if rifampicin resistance is likely.
TB treatment takes months, with several medicines.
TB resistant to rifampicin or other first-line drugs needs special regimens, longer follow-up and expert care.
TB is a leading cause of illness in people with HIV.
A quick list on tb infection control: Open windows for good air flow; Cover coughs and teach cough etiquette.
TB can affect lymph nodes, bones and spine, the brain's lining, the abdomen and other organs.
People living closely with a TB patient, especially children and those with HIV, are at risk.
Common side effects include nausea, rash, joint pain and orange urine.
A quick list on drabc approach: D: check for Danger to you and others; R: check Response, shout and tap.

items.t: Placing a casualty on their side
items.c: A quick list on placing a casualty on their side: Use for unresponsive but breathing casualties; Kneel beside them, place near arm out.
A quick list on stopping heavy bleeding: Apply firm direct pressure with a pad; Keep pressing, do not lift to peek.
A quick list on cooling a burn: Stop the burning and remove from danger; Cool with running water for about 20 minutes.
A quick list on choking in adults: Ask if they can cough or speak; Encourage coughing if airway partly blocked.
Signs include pain, swelling, deformity and inability to use the limb.
Shock means poor blood flow to organs.
Keep the person calm and still, with the bitten limb immobilised at about heart level.
Clear hard objects, cushion the head and loosen tight clothing.
Check the scene is safe and the airway and breathing are ok.
A quick list on five moments for hand hygiene: Before touching a patient; Before a clean or aseptic procedure.
Pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation, often with consciousness level and pain score, show how a patient is doing.
Confirm identity using at least two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, and ask the patient to state them where possible.
Records should be accurate, timely, legible, signed and dated, and describe what was seen and done.
Pressure injuries arise when bony areas are squeezed for too long.
Record all fluids in, orally and by drip, and fluids out, such as urine, drains, vomit and stool.
A quick list on rights of medication safety: Right patient; Right drug.
Assess the patient and the task before moving.
Introduce yourself, use simple words and a calm tone, and let the patient ask questions.
A quick list on handover with sbar: Situation: who and what is happening now; Background: history and what led here.
Health education gives information and skills.
A quick list on stages of behaviour change: Pre-contemplation: not yet thinking of change; Contemplation: weighing it up.
After explaining, ask the patient to say in their own words what they will do.
Community health volunteers live among the people they serve.
Ask about tobacco at each contact, advise clearly to quit, and offer support such as counselling, medicines where available and follow-up.
Regular activity lowers risk of heart disease, diabetes, some cancers and depression.
Heavy alcohol use harms the liver, heart and brain, and raises risks of injury, violence and road crashes.
Road crashes injure many, especially young people and riders of motorcycles.
Income, education, housing, clean water, work and social support strongly shape health.
Health literacy is the ability to find, understand and use health information.
Malnutrition includes undernutrition (wasting, stunting, underweight), micronutrient deficiencies, and overweight or obesity.
Mid-upper arm circumference is measured with a coloured tape, often in children aged six to fifty-nine months.
A balanced diet includes staples for energy, beans or animal foods for protein, fruits and vegetables for vitamins, and some healthy fats, with limited sugar and salt.
From about six months, breast milk alone is no longer enough.
Iron deficiency causes anaemia, tiredness, poor learning and pale skin.
Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, serious eye damage and higher infection risk in children.
A quick list on food hygiene at home: Wash hands before preparing and eating food; Keep raw and cooked foods separate.
Healing needs enough energy, protein, vitamins and minerals.
A quick list on kwashiorkor versus marasmus: Kwashiorkor: swelling of both feet, face, belly; Kwashiorkor: skin and hair changes, irritable.
Prophylactic antibiotics work best when tissue levels are high at the moment of incision.
Some antibiotics wear off during long cases or heavy blood loss.
Many people say they are penicillin allergic but only had a mild rash or stomach upset.
Cephalosporins share a chemical structure with penicillins, so a few allergic patients react to both.
Gentamicin can harm the kidneys and the ears, especially in dehydrated or older patients or with long courses.
Bowel contents contain many anaerobic bacteria.
Vancomycin given too fast can cause flushing, itching and low blood pressure, sometimes called red man syndrome.
When infection is suspected, take wound swabs, pus or blood cultures before starting antibiotics if this does not delay urgent care.
A quick list on why resistance matters: Resistance grows when antibiotics are misused; Unneeded or incomplete courses help it spread.
A quick list on prophylaxis versus treatment: Prophylaxis: prevent infection, usually one dose; Treatment: clear an infection already present.
NSAIDs such as diclofenac and ibuprofen reduce platelet function and can irritate the stomach lining.
A quick list on morphine side effects: Slow breathing and drowsiness; Nausea and vomiting.
Combining different pain medicines works better than one alone and reduces opioid need.
Tramadol is a weaker opioid but still causes nausea, dizziness and drowsiness.
Before breathing stops, patients become very sleepy, hard to rouse, and breathe slowly or shallowly.
A quick list on local anaesthetic toxicity signs: Tingling around the mouth or metallic taste; Ringing in the ears, dizziness.
Ketamine in small doses gives strong pain relief with less effect on breathing than opioids.
Ask patients to rate pain at rest and on movement, using a numbers or faces scale.
Opioids given with benzodiazepines, alcohol or other sedatives add to each other and can depress breathing more than either alone.
A quick list on simple analgesics first: Paracetamol suits most mild to moderate pain; NSAIDs help if kidneys and bleeding risk allow.
Heparin enhances the body's natural clotting inhibitor, antithrombin, so clots form less easily.
Warfarin blocks vitamin K dependent clotting factors.
Warfarin is often stopped several days before planned surgery so the INR falls.
Protamine binds heparin and neutralises it.
Low molecular weight heparin, such as enoxaparin, is used to prevent clots.
Vitamin K helps the liver make clotting factors again, so it reverses warfarin over hours, not minutes.
Rarely, heparin triggers an immune reaction that drops platelets and can paradoxically cause clots.
Direct oral anticoagulants, such as rivaroxaban, do not need regular INR checks and have fewer food interactions.
A quick list on signs of bleeding on anticoagulants: Oozing from wounds or cannula sites; Bruising without clear injury.
A quick list on pre-op anticoagulant questions: Which drug, what dose, and when last taken?; Why is the patient on it?.
Patients who already take beta blockers, such as atenolol, are usually advised to continue them through surgery.
ACE inhibitors and similar drugs can cause low blood pressure after anaesthesia induction.
Digoxin controls heart rate but has a narrow safety range.
Amiodarone treats and prevents many abnormal rhythms, including in cardiac arrest.
Atropine blocks the vagus nerve and speeds the heart.
GTN relaxes blood vessels, easing chest pain and lowering blood pressure.
Some, like amlodipine, mainly relax blood vessels.
Furosemide makes the kidneys pass more urine, which treats fluid overload.
A quick list on vasopressors and inotropes: Vasopressors tighten vessels, raising pressure; Inotropes strengthen the heart's contraction.
Antiplatelet drugs prevent clots in stents and heart disease, but increase bleeding.
Adrenaline is the first-line drug for severe allergic reactions.
In cardiac arrest, adrenaline is given IV or IO at regular intervals according to resuscitation guidelines.
Naloxone blocks opioid receptors and reverses sedation and slow breathing.
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines such as diazepam and midazolam.
Low blood glucose can cause sweating, confusion, seizures or coma, and may be hidden under anaesthesia.
Dantrolene is the key drug for malignant hyperthermia, a rare reaction to some anaesthetic agents.
In severe local anaesthetic toxicity, a lipid emulsion can be given as rescue alongside resuscitation.
Hydrocortisone is used as an adjunct in severe allergic reactions and for patients with adrenal insufficiency under stress.
Salbutamol relaxes airway muscle in wheeze and bronchospasm.
A quick list on crash trolley drug checks: Check seals and expiry dates every day; Keep adrenaline, atropine and amiodarone ready.
Crystalloids, such as saline and Ringer's lactate, are salt solutions that spread through body water.
Normal saline is widely used but large volumes can cause a high chloride acidosis.
Ringer's lactate has electrolytes close to plasma levels.
Choose a straight, soft, visible vein, usually on the forearm or back of the hand.
A quick list on cannula sizes and colours: 14G orange: very fast flow; 16G grey: fast flow, large volumes.
Phlebitis shows as pain, redness, warmth or a hard cord along the vein near the cannula.
If fluid or drug escapes into the surrounding tissue, the site becomes swollen, cold and painful.
Large amounts of air entering a vein can cause serious harm.
Clean your hands, clean the skin, and use a no-touch technique when inserting a cannula.
Many medicines, such as insulin and some muscle relaxants, are stored at about 2 to 8 degrees Celsius.
Opioids and other controlled drugs are kept in a locked cupboard, with keys held by an authorised person.
Some drugs break down in light.
Never use a drug past its expiry date.
Suxamethonium loses potency at room temperature and is usually stored in a fridge.
The cold chain keeps vaccines, insulin and some other products within temperature limits from manufacture to use.
Multi-dose vials can carry contamination if used carelessly.
Oxytocin and ergometrine are often kept cold, and heat can weaken them.
Store similar-looking or similar-sounding drugs apart.
A quick list on daily storage checks: Fridge temperature recorded; Controlled drug count signed.
A quick list on recognising anaphylaxis: Sudden skin flushing, hives or swelling; Wheeze or trouble breathing.
A side effect, like nausea after morphine, is a known and often dose-related effect.
A quick list on malignant hyperthermia warning signs: Rising end-tidal carbon dioxide; Fast heart rate and muscle stiffness.
PONV is more likely in women, non-smokers, those with past PONV or motion sickness, and after opioids.
Itching, especially of the face, is common after spinal or epidural opioids.
Chlorhexidine is common in skin prep, lubricants and some line coatings.
Report any suspected drug reaction through your hospital or national pharmacovigilance system.
A quick list on documenting drug allergies: Name the drug involved; Describe the reaction and its timing.
A headache that worsens when sitting or standing and eases when lying flat may follow a dural puncture.
A quick list on the five rights: Right patient; Right drug.
Some drug names look or sound alike, such as hydralazine and hydroxyzine.
For high-risk drugs such as insulin, heparin, opioids and potassium, two people should check independently.
Label every syringe drawn up outside of immediate use, with drug name, strength and date.
In emergencies, verbal orders are sometimes unavoidable.
A quick list on high-alert medicines: Insulin and heparin; Opioids and sedatives.
A misplaced decimal point can mean ten times too much.
Many doses, especially in children, depend on weight.

items.t: Preparing drugs one at a time
items.c: Draw up, label and use one drug at a time where possible, and never have unlabelled syringes on the tray together.
Before injecting, stop and re-read the label, the patient identity and the allergy status.
Group and screen identifies the blood group and checks for antibodies.
A quick list on abo compatibility: Group O red cells: can go to most patients; Group AB plasma: usually safe for all.
Before transfusion, two trained staff check the patient's identity against the wristband, request form and blood unit label.
Packed red cells increase oxygen-carrying capacity.
Fresh frozen plasma contains clotting factors and is used when bleeding comes with abnormal clotting.
Platelets are given when counts are low or function is poor and there is bleeding or an invasive procedure planned.
Cryoprecipitate is rich in fibrinogen, a key clotting protein.
A quick list on suspected transfusion reaction: Stop the transfusion immediately; Keep the cannula open with saline.
Red cells are stored in a monitored blood fridge, typically at 2 to 6 degrees Celsius.
In major haemorrhage, a massive transfusion protocol delivers red cells, plasma and platelets in set ratios.
Consent is valid when the patient has capacity, receives clear information and agrees freely.
A quick list on four pillars of ethics: Autonomy: respect the patient's choices; Beneficence: act in the patient's best interest.
Capacity is decision-specific and can change.
Write notes at the time, in ink, with date, time, signature and name.
Patients are vulnerable, especially when sedated or anaesthetised.
Mistakes and near misses should be reported promptly through the incident system.
A quick list on scope of practice: Do only what you are trained and authorised to do; Never perform tasks beyond your level to please.
Specimens belong to the patient's record.
A patient with capacity may refuse treatment even if the team disagrees.
Graduates often work in public and private hospitals, mission hospitals, day-surgery units and specialised centres.
Health professionals usually need to register with the relevant regulatory body and renew their licence on time.
A quick list on specialising after your diploma: Sterile services and infection prevention; Endoscopy and minimally invasive surgery.
After a diploma, many learners pursue a higher diploma or degree in a related health field, and later postgraduate study.
Experienced theatre staff can become clinical instructors or tutors.
Private hospitals and day-surgery centres may offer faster pace, newer equipment and different pay structures.
A quick list on building a professional network: Join your professional association; Attend workshops and conferences.
Medical suppliers and manufacturers hire people who understand theatre equipment to demonstrate, train users and support clients.
Surgical camps and outreach programmes give experience with varied cases and limited resources.
Set simple goals: master core scrub and circulating duties, learn two or three specialties, complete continuing education and find a mentor.
A quick list on preparing for day one: Know the ward or theatre location and times; Wear the correct uniform and ID badge.
Theatres are usually arranged in zones: unrestricted, semi-restricted and restricted.
Ask at a quiet moment, not in the middle of a critical step.
Before the case, read about the procedure and the instruments.
Supervisors differ in style, but all want safe, reliable students.
Everyone errs while learning.
A quick list on attachment checklist: Punctuality and full attendance; Correct dress and personal hygiene.
Busy lists mean long standing and little rest.
You may meet severe trauma, death or distressed families.
Before leaving, check that all your cases are signed, return borrowed items and thank the team.
A logbook proves what you have done, not just what you know.

items.t: What to record for each case
items.c: A quick list on what to record for each case: Date and department; Procedure and your role (observed or assisted).
Do not write patient names, phone numbers or full addresses in a logbook or personal notes.
Write entries on the day while details are fresh.
A quick list on observed, assisted, performed: Observed: watched without taking part; Assisted: helped under direct supervision.
A short reflection turns activity into learning.
An unsigned entry may not count.
Programmes often set minimum exposure for case types or skills.
A quick list on keeping the logbook safe: Keep it in a clean, dry, waterproof cover; Do not leave it in clinical areas.
If you make an error, draw one line through it, write the correction and initial it with the date.
List fixed commitments first: classes, attachment, travel and chores.
Reading again feels easy but builds weak memory.
A quick list on spaced revision: Review within one day of learning; Review again after a few days.
Write in your own words, using headings, short lines and simple diagrams.
A mnemonic turns a list into a phrase or picture.
A quick list on group study done well: Choose two to five serious people; Set a topic and time limit beforehand.
Sleep properly, eat a light meal and arrive early with all permitted items.
Underline the command word: list, describe, explain, compare.
Study in a quiet place, phone silent and out of reach.
Learn what the hospital offers, its size, specialties and values.
A quick list on preparing your documents: Clean, updated CV with no gaps unexplained; Certified copies of certificates.
Dress neatly and modestly in clean, plain clothing suited to a health setting.
A quick list on answering with star: Situation: set the scene briefly; Task: say what you had to do.
Give a short summary: who you are, what you trained in, key experience and why you want this role.
Choose a genuine, work-relevant weakness and explain how you are improving it.
Panels may ask what you would do if the count is wrong or an instrument falls.
A quick list on body language: Greet with a steady, friendly voice; Sit upright and keep hands relaxed.
When asked if you have questions, ask something useful: induction, supervision, training or shift patterns.
Leadership is not only for managers.
A team copies what its leader tolerates.
A quick list on delegating safely: Pick someone with the right skills; Explain the task and the expected result.
In an emergency, gather the key facts quickly, state the plan aloud and assign clear tasks.
Give feedback soon, in private and about specific behaviour, not character.
Receiving criticism is hard, but leaders need it.
A quick list on managing theatre resources: Check stock levels before each list; Report shortages early.
Address conflict early, in private and calmly.
A short briefing before the list lets the team share the plan, special risks, equipment needs and who does what.
Remember how new you once felt.
A quick list on the theatre team: Surgeon and assistants; Anaesthetist or anaesthetic staff.
Anyone in the team should feel able to raise a safety concern, whatever their rank.
Before incision, the team usually pauses to confirm patient identity, procedure, site, allergies, antibiotics and equipment.
A quick list on handover well done: Identify the patient and procedure; State the key events and concerns.
Between cases, a fast and safe turnover depends on shared effort.
Cleaners, porters and sterile services staff all protect patients.
Some people are tense or abrupt under pressure.
A brief debrief asks what went well, what did not and what to change next time.
Nurses, doctors, technologists and pharmacists each hold knowledge the others lack.
A quick list on standing and back care: Keep your back straight and knees soft; Shift weight between feet regularly.
Moving patients is a leading cause of staff back injury.
After a sharps injury or splash, wash the area with soap and water or rinse eyes well, do not squeeze or scrub, and report immediately.
Health workers are exposed to blood and respiratory infections.
A quick list on recognising burnout: Constant exhaustion even after rest; Feeling detached or cynical about work.
Regular sleep, meals, movement and time with people you trust protect against stress.
Tired staff make more mistakes.
Theatre staff may meet X-rays, anaesthetic gases, disinfectants and surgical smoke.
Losing a patient or seeing severe injury can leave you shaken.
Long hours and emergencies can swallow personal time.
Many theatre practices, such as skin preparation and warming, are improved by research.
A good question is clear, focused and answerable.
A quick list on types of study: Descriptive: describes what is happening; Cross-sectional: a snapshot at one time.
Use journals, textbooks, guidelines and respected health bodies, and search databases through your library.
Studies with people need ethical approval, voluntary informed consent and protection of privacy.
A sample should represent the group studied.
A quick list on writing a simple proposal: Title and background to the problem; Clear aim and objectives.
Use a tested form or questionnaire, train anyone helping and record data right away.
A result that is statistically significant is not always clinically important, and association is not proof of cause.
Plagiarism is presenting another person's words or ideas as your own.
An acute abdomen is sudden severe abdominal pain that may need surgery.
A quick list on signs of peritonitis: Rigid, board-like abdomen; Pain worse on movement or coughing.
Bowel obstruction causes colicky pain, vomiting, swelling of the abdomen and failure to pass wind or stool.
A hernia that becomes tense, painful, tender and cannot be pushed back may have its blood supply cut off.
Typical appendicitis begins with vague central pain that moves to the right lower abdomen, with loss of appetite, nausea and low fever.
A perforated ulcer causes sudden intense upper abdominal pain and a rigid abdomen as stomach contents leak out.
A quick list on volvulus and the twisted gut: Bowel twists around its own mesentery; Blood supply may be cut off.
A quick list on preparing for emergency laparotomy: Consent, or documented emergency decision; Group and crossmatch blood.
Bleeding after surgery may be seen in drains and dressings or hidden inside the body.
Dehiscence means the wound edges separate, often a week or so after surgery.
Pain, anaesthesia, opioids and fear can stop the bladder emptying.
After abdominal surgery the bowel can pause, causing bloating, vomiting and no passage of wind or stool.
A quick list on atelectasis and chest care: Small areas of lung can collapse after surgery; Shallow breathing from pain is a common cause.
A quick list on pressure injury prevention: Pad bony areas on the theatre table; Avoid dragging; lift or use a slide sheet.
A quick list on types of wound: Abrasion: scraped surface; Laceration: torn or cut skin.
Check bleeding, depth, size, contamination and the injured limb's circulation, movement and sensation.
Apply firm direct pressure with a clean pad and raise the limb if possible.
Irrigation washes out dirt and bacteria and is one of the best ways to reduce infection.
Primary closure means closing a clean fresh wound straight away with sutures, staples, glue or strips.
For contaminated or high-risk wounds, surgeons may leave the wound open, dress it and close it after several days if there are no signs of infection.
A quick list on choosing a dressing: Keep the wound moist but not soaking; Protect from dirt and further injury.
Dirty, deep or puncture wounds can lead to tetanus.
Human and animal bites carry many germs and are usually cleaned thoroughly and not closed tightly.
A quick list on stages of wound healing: Haemostasis: clotting stops bleeding; Inflammation: cleaning and defence.
Remove the person from danger, put out flames and take off burnt clothing and jewellery unless stuck to the skin.
A quick list on burn depth classification: Superficial: red, dry, painful; Partial thickness: blisters, moist, very painful.
The rule of nines gives a quick estimate of the body surface burnt in adults.
A quick list on airway burns warning signs: Burns to the face, mouth or neck; Singed nose hairs or soot around the nose.
Large burns leak fluid from the circulation, causing shock.
Burns, and especially dressing changes, are very painful.
Burnt skin loses its barrier, so infection is a major danger.
A quick list on chemical burns: Remove contaminated clothing; Brush off dry powder before flushing.
Electrical injury may look small on the skin but damage muscle, nerves and the heart underneath.
Deep circumferential burns can form a hard tight crust that restricts circulation in a limb or breathing in the chest.
In an open fracture the bone or a wound communicates with the break.
A quick list on compartment syndrome signs: Pain out of proportion to the injury; Pain on stretching the muscles.
Splint the limb in the position found, unless the circulation is threatened.
Traction applies a steady pull to line up broken bones, relieve muscle spasm and reduce pain until surgery.
Pelvic fractures can cause heavy hidden bleeding.
